title: VPC regulatory rapid response playbook
summary: Concise rapid-response messaging and scripts for sales/solutions when a regulated buyer asks for evidence on VPC/private control plane, data flows, and audit artifacts. Designed for short pre-meeting prep and live objection handling.
body:
Purpose:
This is a lean, battle-tested playbook for customer-facing teams (AE, SE, Solutions, CS) to handle high-stakes regulatory and audit questions about Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) — with an emphasis on control plane expectations, evidence bundles, and converting the ask into a pilot. It is intentionally short, scriptable, and focused on the first 72 hours of a regulated buyer engagement.

Primary audiences and use cases:
- CISO/Head of InfoSec: evidence-oriented objections about data residency, key custody, and audit logs.
- Compliance/Pull teams (internal audit, legal): want artifacts and process descriptions.
- Platform/Infra buyers evaluating operational separation and failover.
- Sales/SE prepping for a compliance-focused RFP or security review.

Core positioning pillars (short lines to use in meetings):
1) We separate the control plane from customer data paths and offer deploy-time choices — managed control plane (VPC peered with customer), customer-hosted control plane, or fully air-gapped on prem.
2) Evidence-first: we provide packaged artifact sets (config snapshots, audit logs, KMS attestations, SRE runbooks) to satisfy most audit requests within 10 business days.
3) Predictable operations: SLA-backed Dedicated tenants and documented fallback rules for model routing and data-independent health checks.
4) Least-privilege default: default deployments remove any data-plane egress to Redwood-hosted services unless explicitly enabled by the customer.

Quick objection-response library (sound bites + longer reply if asked to escalate):
Objection A: "We can't allow an external control plane to store metadata about requests."
- Short: "Understood — our Private options let you run a control plane in your VPC or on-prem, where metadata stays in your network. We map our orchestration to your IAM and KMS."
- Evidence to offer: architecture diagram (network flows), sample IAM policies, and a short audit extract showing no persistent request payload retention in the control plane.

Objection B: "How do we know tokens/keys are not duplicated in Redwood logs?"
- Short: "We never persist raw keys/tokens in logs in Private mode; logs are truncated and tokenized by default. We also support customer-managed KMS so key material never leaves your control."
- Evidence to offer: sample syslog redaction config, KMS integration diagram, and a short excerpt from our SOC-equivalent runbook on secrets handling.

Objection C: "Can you prove you meet our audit requirements (retention, immutability, chain-of-custody)?"
- Short: "Yes — we deliver an evidence bundle aligned to common standards (ISO/SOC/PCI-adjacent artifacts) tailored to your controls mapping. We will scope a joint artifact checklist on day one of a pilot."
- Evidence to offer: checklist template, example immutable S3 bucket policy and snapshot of object versioning, signed attestations for patch levels.

Competitive short-calls (how to position versus two common archetypes):
- Against big cloud-managed LLM endpoints: "They offer scale, we offer purpose-built evidence and a pluggable control plane you can own. If your requirement is auditability and isolation, our Private tier reduces compliance cost by narrowing the trust boundary."
- Against pure self-hosted inference vendors: "Self-hosted gives control but also maintenance overhead. With Redwood Private you get a minimal, customer-owned control plane and handoffs: we automate ops templates, upgrade windows, and provide runbooks so your SREs maintain control without building every integration."

Rapid evidence bundles (what to include for first delivery):
- Architecture diagram (3 slides) showing: data plane flows, control plane placement, KMS flow, network ACLs and peering.
- Config snapshot: one example terraform/module snippet for VPC peering and security groups.
- Audit/log sample: redacted control plane audit log showing start/stop events and no payload retention.
- KMS proof: example CMK ARN and policy snippet showing external KMS integration.
- SLA + runbook excerpt: uptime targets for Dedicated and failover policy notes.
- Personnel & process: list of roles with access levels for pilot and contact for escalation.

Scripts: 60-second CISO opener (two variants)
- Variant A (risk-focused): "I appreciate the need for concrete artifacts. Our approach is to minimize the trust surface — you can run our control plane inside your VPC, connect to your KMS, and receive a curated evidence bundle within the first 10 business days of the pilot so your audit team can validate behaviors rather than policy claims. Can I confirm your primary artifact requirement is immutability of logs or KMS key custody?"
- Variant B (process-focused): "We've structured pilots so your audit team gets a hands-on checklist mapped to common frameworks. We'll nominate a single SE to work the checklist with you and deliver the artifact pack within the pilot window. Does that sound like the right approach?"

Pilot ask templates (two short email snippets)
- Short pilot invite (technical): "Hi <Name>, we'd like to propose a 4-week pilot: deploy Redwood Private control plane into your staging VPC, configure KMS hookup, run 10k inference tokens/day for workload fidelity, and deliver an evidence bundle for your audit team in week 3. Please confirm a primary technical contact and a read-only service account for the trial. — Sofia"
- Short pilot invite (executive): "Hi <Name>, proposed pilot scope: validate control plane placement, key custody, and audit artifacts. Expect a short artifacts package and a 45-minute review with our solutions team. Proposed start week: <date>. Approve or suggest alternate window? — Sofia"

Escalation map (if buyer asks for compliance letters / pen test results):
- Level 1 (SE): provide architecture, config snippets, log extracts.
- Level 2 (Security lead): attach redacted pen-test summary and incident response runbook; schedule 1:1 with buyer's security team.
- Level 3 (Security Director / Legal): provide contract language draft, SOC2-type summary, or facilitate an NDA for deeper artifact exchange.

Notes on framing 'control plane' language (what to say, what to avoid):
- Say: "control plane placement or mode" (keep neutral), "customer-controlled keys", "no customer data persisted by default", "audit artifact pack", "minimal privileged services".
- Avoid: technical jargon-heavy words alone (e.g., 'orchestration' without context), absolutes like 'zero chance' or 'no risk', and product-internal names that leak roadmap assumptions.

Common audit checklist (starter mapping to buyer asks)
- Data residency: describe which surfaces store data, retention policies, and region controls.
- Key custody: KMS integration, CMK controls, rotation policy.
- Access control: IAM role lists, RBAC table, emergency access process.
- Logging & immutability: log sinks, retention, versioning, and hash-based integrity checks.
- Patch & configuration management: OS/agent versions, patch cadence, and CVE remediation timelines.

Tactical tips for meetings:
- Bring artifacts to the first call (one-pagers), not just promises. Buyers in regulated industries evaluate behavior, not claims.
- Offer a narrow single-question pilot first (e.g., KMS hookup + log sample) to build confidence.
- Use the checklist during the meeting to capture additional evidence requests and set explicit due dates.
- If the buyer brings up a competitor, immediately ask which specific control or artifact they need that you haven't shown; convert that into the next short deliverable.

Appendix: one-paragraph competitive snippets for internal use (copy-paste ready)
- Big cloud provider: "Good for scale, but typically requires customers to stitch together audit artifacts across services. We provide an opinionated evidence pack and optional control plane placement so your compliance review is single-vendor for inference."
- Self-hosted solution: "Full control but longer time-to-value and heavier SRE ownership; Redwood Private reduces operational lift with deployment templates and curated runbooks while keeping control in the customer's hands."

Last steps checklist before sending evidence pack:
1) Sanitize logs (automated script).
2) Redact any customer-identifying content.
3) Freeze config snapshot and sign with an approver.
4) Attach a brief explanation mapping artifacts to buyer controls.
5) Propose next review date and clear owner.

Owner notes (internal):
- This doc is intentionally condensed — keep it updated with two new artifacts we generate per quarter: (1) updated KMS proof sample, (2) pen-test executive summary redaction template.
- Track downstream asks in JIRA (linked artifact above) so we can reuse generated evidence.

End of playbook.
